title: The Pour Is Decided Before the First Truck
summary: A good concrete mix becomes good concrete only if it is placed into correct forms over correctly set steel, consolidated, cured and left supported until it is strong enough. Each of those steps is invisible once the concrete hardens, so the pour is really decided by a pre-pour inspection and by the stripping and reshoring rules. Learn the sequence and you can run a pour day as owner.
body:
By the time the first truck arrives, the quality of a concrete pour has mostly been decided, by the forms, the steel, the embeds and the plan for curing and support, so the owner's leverage lives in the inspection before the pour and the rules for what happens after it.

Recall

Q. In the substitution meeting, why did slag cement need a check on the stripping plan?

A. Because slag slows early strength gain, which can delay when forms may be stripped and lengthen the floor cycle, eating the saving.

Q. What is downdrag on a pile?

A. Added downward load from a settling soil layer around the pile, so the soil hangs on the pile instead of supporting it.

Q. In an electrical system, what distinguishes emergency power from optional standby?

A. Emergency power serves life-safety loads such as egress lighting and is held to the strictest requirements; optional standby serves loads the owner chooses to keep running, with lighter rules.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week Ingrid taught that concrete is a recipe with a contract attached. This week the recipe leaves the chute and becomes structure. That transition happens in a few hours, is done by a crew under time pressure, and is permanent. You cannot inspect consolidation after the fact without drilling holes, you cannot add cover once the slab has set, and you cannot undo a slab that was stripped too soon. The pour is also the most dangerous routine activity on a concrete frame: formwork and shoring carry tons of wet concrete, workers and equipment, and when they fail, they fail suddenly. Duke's job, and yours as owner, is to make sure every pour starts from a verified state and ends with a defined plan.

The pre-pour inspection

In plain English: before any concrete goes in, someone qualified walks the deck and confirms everything that will be buried is right.

The professional framing is the pre-pour inspection, often recorded on a pour card or pour release: a form that each responsible party signs to confirm its work is ready. Typical items are formwork dimensions, line and level; form ties and bracing; reinforcing bar size, spacing, laps and cover, set on chairs that will survive foot traffic; embedded items such as electrical conduit, sleeves for pipes, anchor bolts, post-tensioning tendons and their profile where used; block-outs for openings; cleanliness of the forms; and the special inspector's sign-off on reinforcing. The mechanical, electrical and plumbing trades sign that their sleeves and conduits are in and correct, because a sleeve missed today becomes a core drill through finished structure next month.

Applied example, hypothetical. A slab pour of 300 cubic yards is scheduled for 6 a.m. At 3 p.m. the day before, the inspector finds that 40 feet of slab edge has 1.25 inches of cover where 2 inches is specified, and the plumbing sleeves for one riser are missing. Both are fixed by 7 p.m., re-inspected and signed. Cost: a few crew hours. If found after the pour, the cover defect means a durability remedy for that edge, and the missing sleeves mean core drilling, with the risk of cutting reinforcing steel or tendons, and an engineer's review. Pre-pour hours are the cheapest hours on the job.

Placing, consolidation and curing

Placing means getting concrete into the forms without separating it: limiting free-fall height, avoiding long horizontal flow, and placing in layers. Consolidation means removing trapped air, usually with internal vibrators, so the concrete fills around the steel and against the forms. Under-vibration leaves voids, called honeycombing; over-vibration can separate paste from stone. Finishing follows for slabs.

Curing means keeping the concrete moist and at a suitable temperature long enough for the cement to keep reacting. Concrete that dries out early stops gaining strength near the surface, shrinks and cracks, and becomes more permeable, which undoes the low water ratio Ingrid fought for. Curing methods include wet coverings, ponding, curing compounds sprayed on the surface and leaving forms in place. ACI 308 is the curing reference many specifications draw on. In hot, windy, dry conditions, evaporation can pull water off the surface faster than it rises, causing plastic shrinkage cracks within hours, so curing starts immediately after finishing, not the next morning.

Say that out loud now.

Formwork, shoring and reshoring

In plain English: forms hold wet concrete in shape, shores hold the forms up, and once the forms come off, temporary posts called reshores keep supporting the young slab while floors above are built.

In a multi-storey concrete frame, a newly poured slab cannot carry itself, let alone the next floor's wet concrete and formwork. So the loads of construction are shared through shores and reshores down through several floors of young concrete. The sequence, how many floors are reshored and when each level may be stripped, is a temporary works design. It depends on the concrete actually reaching a minimum strength in place, not on the calendar.

Applied example, hypothetical. The engineer specifies that slab forms may be stripped when the concrete reaches 75 percent of its specified strength, confirmed by field-cured cylinders, which are cylinders cured on the slab beside the concrete rather than in the laboratory. In summer the slab reaches that in 4 days. In a cool spell it takes 7. A crew working to a 4-day calendar strips early in the cool week. That is the exact mechanism of this week's failure case.

Low breaks

A low break, a cylinder result below what was required, triggers the investigation Ivo described last week: check the testing, check the design margin, then test in place if needed. On pour day, your job is simpler: make sure the cylinders are made correctly, from the right trucks, and cured as specified, because a bad cylinder starts an expensive investigation into good concrete.

How the best do it

Well-run concrete frame builders treat the pour card as a hard hold point: no truck is called until every signature is on it. Many also post the stripping and reshoring sequence on the deck as a drawing, so the crew sees which shores must stay and which may come out. A small developer can copy both at no cost: make the pour card a contract hold point, and require the reshoring drawing on site before any stripping.

One more owner habit, Mr Shabazz: ask to see the pour card for the last three pours whenever you visit site. Not the summary, the cards. A card with every line signed and dated before the trucks were called tells you the system is working. A card signed in one hand, or signed after the pour time, tells you it is not, and you have found that out before it matters.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is stripping or removing reshores on the calendar instead of on verified strength. The control is a written rule: no stripping without field-cured cylinder results, or another approved in-place test, meeting the engineer's stated stripping strength, against a reshoring drawing.

The beginner's mistake

Watching the pour and skipping the pre-pour. The pour is noisy and impressive; the pre-pour is quiet and decides the outcome.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: remedial work after a defective pour may be treated differently from original construction; ask your tax adviser and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: formwork failures injure workers, and owners can face claims, so contracts must allocate temporary works design clearly to the contractor. Banking: the lender's monitor will want pour records and test results before certifying structural progress. Governance: stripping and reshoring rules should be in the contract, not left to habit. Estate: documented structure is easier to hold and transfer. Exit: buyers' engineers look for honeycombing, cracking and cover, and the pour records answer their questions.

Callback

In Week 53, Duke taught the OSHA Focus Four hazards and the multi-employer doctrine. Formwork collapse is the struck-by and caught-in hazard at its worst, and the multi-employer doctrine means the owner's choices about schedule pressure can matter to who is responsible.

Recap

The pour card verifies everything buried before concrete arrives. Placing, consolidation and curing turn the mix into structure. Shores and reshores carry construction loads through young floors, and stripping follows verified strength, never the calendar. Good cylinders prevent false alarms.

Next: Ford, on Failure Forensics: the Skyline Towers collapse of 1973.
checklist: Every pour has a pour card signed by each responsible party before trucks are called.
The inspector checks cover, steel, embeds and sleeves before every pour.
Placing and vibration methods are agreed for each pour.
Curing starts immediately after finishing and is recorded.
A reshoring drawing is on site before any stripping.
Stripping follows field-cured cylinder results against the engineer's stated strength.
Cylinders are made and cured correctly to avoid false low breaks.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and the contractor's temporary works engineer.
head: Field checklist
speak: By the time the first truck arrives, the pour is mostly decided. Before every pour, the inspector and each trade sign a pour card confirming forms, steel, cover, embeds and sleeves are right, because everything inside is buried for good. In a hypothetical case, thin cover and missing sleeves found the afternoon before cost a few crew hours to fix; found after the pour, they would mean a durability remedy and core drilling. During the pour, concrete is placed without separation and vibrated to remove voids, and curing starts right after finishing. Afterwards, shores and reshores carry construction loads through several young floors, and forms come off only when field-cured cylinders show the stripping strength the engineer specified, never on a calendar. That rule is what this week's failure case teaches.
terms: Pre-pour inspection — the check of forms, reinforcing, cover and embedded items before concrete is placed, often recorded on a signed pour card.
Reshoring — temporary posts placed under a slab after its forms are stripped, so it keeps support while floors above are built.
Field-cured cylinder — a test cylinder cured on site beside the structure, used to estimate the strength of the concrete in place.

hostile.q: I'm the general contractor. We're two days behind. We'll strip the deck at four days like last month. Why do you need cylinder results?
hostile.a: Because last month was warm and this week is not, and concrete gains strength with temperature, not with dates. The engineer's stripping strength is 75 percent of specified, measured on field-cured cylinders. If today's breaks show it, strip today and I will help you recover the days elsewhere. If they do not, the forms stay and we look at other ways to recover time, such as more form sets or a crew shift. I will not trade two days for a slab carrying load it cannot yet hold.

title: Skyline Towers, 1973: Stripped Before It Was Strong
summary: On 2 March 1973, an apartment building under construction at Bailey's Crossroads in Fairfax County, Virginia, collapsed after shores were removed from an upper floor of young concrete, killing fourteen workers. Seven forensic steps show how a routine schedule decision became a progressive collapse. The lesson is that stripping follows verified strength, never the calendar.
body:
At Skyline Towers in 1973, forms and shores came out from under concrete that was not yet strong enough to carry what was above it, the floor failed, and the floors below could not stop the falling weight, so a routine stripping decision became a collapse that killed fourteen workers.

Recall

Q. What is a field-cured cylinder?

A. A test cylinder cured on site beside the structure, so its strength estimates the concrete in place rather than concrete in ideal laboratory conditions.

Q. What is the root cause in the Millennium Tower case?

A. A foundation whose performance depended on predicted long-term clay consolidation and stable surroundings, without margin or a monitoring and response plan to match.

Q. What is commissioning in MEP systems?

A. The documented process of verifying that systems are installed and perform as the owner's requirements state, through functional and integrated testing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I will keep to the facts I am confident of. On 2 March 1973 a residential tower under construction at Skyline Center, at Bailey's Crossroads in Fairfax County, Virginia, collapsed during construction. Fourteen workers were killed and dozens injured. The National Bureau of Standards, the federal agency now called the National Institute of Standards and Technology, investigated. Its central finding concerned shores removed from beneath a recently placed floor before the concrete had developed enough strength. I will not quote figures from the report that I cannot confirm. The mechanism is what you need.

1. Timeline

The building was a cast-in-place concrete frame rising floor by floor, each floor formed, reinforced, poured and then supported while the next went up. On the day of the collapse, work was under way near the top of the frame, with shores being removed from a floor of recently placed concrete in late-winter conditions, which slow strength gain. A section of that floor failed. Its weight and debris fell onto the floors below, which were not designed to arrest a falling floor, and the failure progressed down through the structure, also damaging an attached parking structure.

2. Key decisions

The decisive decision was when to remove shores, made on the basis of schedule rather than measured in-place strength. Behind it sat a second decision: how stripping and reshoring were planned, documented and supervised, and whether anyone had authority and evidence to stop it.

3. Assumptions

The working assumption was that concrete a certain number of days old is strong enough. That holds in warm weather and fails in cold, because strength gain slows sharply at low temperatures. A second assumption was that the floors below could catch a failure above. Floors are designed for their own service loads, not for the impact of a falling floor plus its formwork.

4. Incentives

A concrete frame is priced and scheduled on its floor cycle: the number of days to form, pour and strip each level. Formwork is reused upward, so every day the forms stay on one floor is a day the next floor waits. Contractors, crews and owners all benefit from a faster cycle. Nobody earns anything from leaving shores in an extra day. The incentive points one way, which is why the rule must point the other.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

The cold weather was itself the warning. Any concrete frame working through cold days must expect slower strength gain and adjust the stripping schedule. A stripping decision taken without strength evidence for that specific floor, in those specific conditions, is a decision without data. On sites like this, the absence of field-cured cylinder results, or of any other in-place strength evidence, is the warning sign.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the removal of support from that floor. Before it, the remedy was to wait. After it, a floor too weak to carry its load had nothing beneath it, and once it began to fail, the floors below had no capacity to stop the falling mass. Progressive collapse means that past a certain point nothing a crew can do changes the outcome.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a construction process in which support was removed on time rather than on strength, without in-place strength evidence or an engineered reshoring plan enforced on site. The cold weather turned a routine practice into a fatal one.

The rule after the case

Modern practice responds directly. OSHA's concrete construction standard requires that forms and shores not be removed until the employer determines the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads, based on specified tests or plans; verify the current text of Subpart Q of 29 CFR Part 1926 before relying on it. Specifications set a stripping strength, verified by field-cured cylinders or approved in-place methods. Reshoring is engineered and drawn. The structural engineer of record states the strength criteria; the contractor's temporary works engineer designs the shoring and reshoring; the owner's inspector checks that results exist before stripping.

What it means for an owner

You will not strip forms yourself, Mr Shabazz, but your schedule creates the pressure that leads to early stripping. When you push a floor cycle, ask how the cycle holds in cold weather and what evidence governs stripping. Budget for extra form sets or longer cycles in cold months rather than assuming summer rates all year. And make sure your contract says no stripping without strength evidence, so that the contractor's supervisor has the authority to wait.

Why the floors below could not save it

One idea from this case deserves a second look, Mr Shabazz, because it overturns an intuition. Most people assume that if one floor fails, the floor beneath will catch it. It will not, for two reasons. First, a floor is designed for a distributed load at rest: its own weight, finishes and the people and furniture in service. A falling floor arrives as an impact, a load many times larger than its weight at rest, concentrated where the debris lands. Second, during construction the floors below are themselves young, partly loaded by reshores and not yet at full strength. So each floor that is hit is weaker than its design assumes and is struck by more than its design allows. That is why the failure ran downward.

The lesson for the owner is that a concrete frame under construction is at its most fragile. The building you will eventually own, with every floor cured, connected and at strength, is far more robust than the skeleton standing on any given day of the build. The rules for stripping and reshoring exist to carry the skeleton safely through that fragile period.

What the investigation teaches about evidence

The federal investigation could reconstruct what happened because physical evidence and records existed: the failed concrete, the sequence of work, the shores. On your projects, the equivalent evidence is created every day: field-cured cylinder results, the reshoring drawing, the stripping log stating which level was stripped when and on what strength result. If that log does not exist, nobody can prove the stripping decision was made on evidence, and in an accident that absence speaks loudly. Ask for the stripping log on every site visit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a schedule that assumes every floor reaches stripping strength in the same number of days. The control is strength-based stripping, written into the contract, with field-cured cylinders and a reshoring drawing.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking formwork is the contractor's problem only. The contractor designs it; the owner's schedule loads it.

Callback

In Week 103, Bram taught progressive collapse: a local failure that spreads beyond proportion. Skyline Towers shows that the most vulnerable time for progressive collapse is during construction, when concrete is young and the structure is incomplete.

Recap

Shores came out from a young floor in cold weather, the floor failed, and the collapse progressed. Fourteen workers died. The cause was time-based stripping without strength evidence. Rule 113 makes strength, not the calendar, the trigger.

Next: Roman, on The Money: the floor cycle, and what a wait costs against what a tear-out costs.
checklist: My contract forbids stripping without in-place strength evidence.
The engineer of record states the stripping and reshoring strength criteria.
The contractor's temporary works engineer designs shoring and reshoring.
A reshoring drawing is posted on site before stripping.
Field-cured cylinders are made for every floor that will be stripped.
My schedule allows longer floor cycles or extra form sets in cold weather.
The site supervisor has written authority to delay stripping.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and temporary works engineer.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 2 March 1973, an apartment tower under construction at Bailey's Crossroads in Fairfax County, Virginia, collapsed. Fourteen workers were killed. The National Bureau of Standards found that shores had been removed from a recently placed floor before its concrete had enough strength, in late-winter conditions that slow strength gain. The floor failed and the falling weight carried through the floors below. The incentive in a concrete frame always favours a faster floor cycle, so the rule has to push the other way. The root cause was removing support on time rather than on strength, without in-place evidence or an enforced reshoring plan. Rule 113: never strip forms or remove reshores on a calendar; strip only when field-cured cylinders or an approved in-place test meet the engineer's stated strength, against an engineered reshoring plan.
terms: Progressive collapse — a failure in which the loss of one element spreads to others, so a local failure becomes a disproportionate one.
Floor cycle — the number of working days to form, reinforce, pour and strip one floor of a concrete frame.
Stripping strength — the minimum in-place concrete strength the engineer requires before forms may be removed.

hostile.q: I'm the safety officer for the contractor. Your schedule assumes a four-day floor cycle all year. How do you expect us to meet that in winter without stripping early?
hostile.a: I do not. A four-day cycle is a warm-weather number, and the contract already says stripping follows field-cured cylinder results against the engineer's strength, not the calendar. If winter strength gain is slower, we either accept a longer cycle in those weeks or add a second set of forms, and I will fund the choice that protects the schedule best. What nobody on this job will do is strip a floor without its strength results, and your supervisor has my written support to wait.

rule: Rule 113: Never strip forms or remove reshores on a calendar; strip only when field-cured cylinders or an approved in-place test meet the engineer's stated strength, against an engineered reshoring plan posted on site.

title: The Floor Cycle: What Waiting Costs and What Tearing Out Costs
summary: A concrete frame's cost and schedule are driven by its floor cycle, so every day of waiting for strength has a price. So does a pour that has to be removed and replaced. Pricing both shows that the safe choices, extra form sets, cold-weather measures and strength-based stripping, are usually cheaper than they look.
body:
The floor cycle is the heartbeat of a concrete frame, every extra day in it has a price you can calculate, and that price is almost always smaller than the cost of a single pour that has to be cut out and replaced.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Skyline Towers collapse?

A. Removing support from a young floor on time rather than on verified strength, without in-place evidence or an enforced reshoring plan, in cold weather.

Q. Why do long piles cost more than extra feet times rate?

A. Because they slow the rig and move the critical path, adding general conditions and interest carry.

Q. What is a chiller's role in a central cooling system?

A. It produces chilled water that is pumped to air handlers or fan coils, where it absorbs heat and moisture from the air.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the structure of a mid-rise concrete building is a repeated pattern: the same floor built many times. That makes its schedule and cost unusually predictable, and unusually sensitive to one number, the floor cycle. When a contractor proposes to save time, it is usually by shortening that cycle. When the weather slows strength gain, it lengthens. You need to price both directions so that the safe decision is also a decision you can defend on money.

What one day of the cycle costs

In plain English: if each floor takes one more day, the whole frame takes one more day per floor, and the building finishes that much later.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A frame of 10 repeating floors runs a 5-working-day cycle: 50 working days for the typical floors. The frame is on the critical path. General conditions run 60,000 dollars a week, 12,000 dollars a working day. The construction loan is about half drawn during the frame, at 15,000,000 dollars, with interest at a hypothetical 8 percent a year, about 3,300 dollars per calendar day, call it 4,600 dollars per working day once weekends are counted. A day of delay therefore costs about 16,600 dollars.

If cold weather adds 2 days to each of 4 floors, that is 8 working days, about 133,000 dollars. Alternatively, a second set of slab forms at a hypothetical 60,000 dollars of rental and labour lets the crew start the next floor while the first set waits for strength. If it saves 6 of the 8 days, it recovers about 100,000 dollars for 60,000 dollars spent. That is a trade worth making, and it is safe.

What a tear-out costs

Now the other side. Suppose a slab is stripped early, deflects and cracks, or a pour has to be removed because of low strength and poor consolidation confirmed by cores. Removal and replacement of one slab section, hypothetically 2,000 square feet: demolition and disposal 60,000 dollars, new forms, steel and concrete 80,000 dollars, engineering and testing 20,000 dollars, total 160,000 dollars. Add the delay: the floors above wait, perhaps 10 working days, about 166,000 dollars. A tear-out of one section costs about 326,000 dollars, more than the entire cold-weather cost above. A collapse is not in the same arithmetic at all, because lives are not a cost line.

Say that out loud now.

Cold-weather and hot-weather measures as investments

Measures that keep strength gain on schedule have a price too. In cold weather: heated enclosures, insulated blankets, accelerating admixtures, warmer concrete from the plant. In hot weather: chilled water or ice in the mix, retarders, night pours, evaporation control and immediate curing. Each costs money per pour. Compare it with the days it saves at 16,600 dollars a day and with the risk it removes. Blankets and an accelerator that save 2 days on a floor for 8,000 dollars are a clear win. Measures that save nothing, because strength was not the constraint, are waste.

How the lender reads the cycle

The lender's monitor tracks frame progress against the schedule. A cycle that is lengthening shows up in the monitor's report and in the interest reserve, because a later finish means more months of interest. A monitor who sees the owner choosing a second form set over early stripping reads competence. A monitor who sees a slab tear-out reads a quality system problem and starts testing everything more closely, which costs you time on every later draw.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: delay is a quiet transfer of value from your equity to your lender and your contractor, through interest and general conditions. Spending a known sum to protect the cycle safely is usually a better use of capital than accepting an unknown delay. But do not fund structural fixes from your personal liquidity floor; hold a construction contingency that can carry them. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal funding decision.

Worked example two: the shortened cycle proposal

Now the opposite proposal, Mr Shabazz. The contractor offers to cut the cycle from 5 days to 4 for a fee, by using an accelerating admixture, a high-early-strength mix and a third form set, and asks for a 90,000 dollar change. Over 10 floors, one day saved per floor is 10 working days, worth about 166,000 dollars at 16,600 a day. On money alone, it looks good.

Then ask three questions. One: does the faster mix still meet the exposure limits and durability requirements the engineer set? High-early-strength mixes can bring more heat and shrinkage, so the engineer must approve. Two: does stripping still follow field-cured strength, or does the faster cycle assume the strength will always be there on day 4? The faster mix makes that more likely, but cold days still exist. Three: does the reshoring sequence still work with more floors of younger concrete loaded at once? If the answers are yes, yes and yes, the trade earns about 76,000 dollars net. If any answer is no, the saving is borrowed from structural safety or durability and is not a saving at all.

That is the general shape of any schedule acceleration in a concrete frame: price it, then check whether it is achieved by better methods or by thinner margins. The first is a good trade. The second is a deferred cost with a large and uncertain price.

Put the comparison on one page for the decision log, Mr Shabazz: the proposal, its price, the days it saves, the value of those days, and the three answers from the engineer. A partner reading it sees at once that the saving was tested against safety and durability, not merely accepted. And when the next acceleration proposal arrives, you have a template that takes ten minutes to fill in.

One more cost belongs on that page: the cost of the evidence itself. Field-cured cylinders, extra laboratory breaks at early ages and an inspector on site for stripping cost a few thousand dollars over a frame. They are the cheapest line in this lesson and the one that makes every other line safe to rely on.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a schedule built on summer cycle times for every month of the year, which creates pressure to strip early. The control is a seasonal cycle assumption in the schedule, with a budget for form sets and weather measures.

The beginner's mistake

Counting only the general conditions cost of delay and forgetting interest, which grows as the loan is drawn.

Callback

In Week 50, Petra taught the critical path and float ownership. The floor cycle is the critical path for most of a concrete frame, so every day in it is a day on the finish date, and there is no float to absorb a stripping shortcut gone wrong.

Recap

A day on the floor cycle costs general conditions plus interest. Weather slows strength gain and lengthens the cycle. Extra form sets and weather measures often recover more than they cost. A tear-out costs more than the delay it was meant to avoid.

Next: REGA, on The Rules: OSHA, ACI and who is responsible for formwork and reshoring.
checklist: I know the planned floor cycle and which floors fall in cold or hot weeks.
I know what one working day of frame delay costs, including interest.
I price a second form set against the days it saves.
I price cold- and hot-weather measures against the days they save.
I compare the cost of waiting with the cost of a tear-out.
My schedule uses seasonal cycle times, not summer rates all year.
Structural fixes are funded from project contingency, not my liquidity floor.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record for any removal and replacement.
head: Field checklist
speak: A concrete frame repeats one floor many times, so its cost hinges on the floor cycle. In a hypothetical case, a working day of frame delay costs about 12,000 dollars of general conditions and about 4,600 of interest, so roughly 16,600 dollars. Cold weather adding 2 days to 4 floors costs about 133,000. A second form set for 60,000 that recovers 6 of those days returns about 100,000, so it pays. Compare a tear-out: removing and replacing one 2,000 square foot section is about 160,000 dollars, plus 10 days of delay, about 326,000 in total. Weather measures are investments to test against the days they save. So I schedule seasonal cycle times, budget form sets and weather measures, and never let a summer schedule create pressure to strip early.
terms: General conditions — the contractor's time-related site costs such as staff, offices, cranes, temporary services and insurance.
Accelerating admixture — a chemical added to concrete to speed early strength gain, often used in cold weather.
Tear-out — removal and replacement of defective construction, here a section of concrete slab.

hostile.q: I'm the lender's monitor. Your frame is running two days a floor behind in winter. Why are you paying for a second set of forms instead of pushing the contractor to strip faster?
hostile.a: Because stripping faster in cold weather is how frames fail, and the specification makes stripping follow field-cured strength results. A second form set at about 60,000 dollars recovers roughly 6 of the 8 days we were losing, worth about 100,000 dollars in general conditions and interest. It is drawn from the construction contingency, and the updated cost to complete and schedule are in this month's package for you to test.

title: Who Owns the Shores: OSHA, ACI and Responsibility for Formwork
summary: OSHA's construction standards govern formwork, shoring and their removal as a matter of worker safety. ACI guidance and the project specification govern the engineering and the strength criteria. The contract decides who designs temporary works and who checks them. Know where each rule lives so responsibility is never ambiguous on pour day.
body:
Formwork and reshoring sit where three sets of rules meet, OSHA for worker safety, ACI and the specification for engineering and strength, and the contract for who designs and who checks, and accidents happen in the gaps between them.

Recall

Q. In the floor cycle example, why did the second form set pay for itself?

A. It let work continue on the next floor while the first set waited for strength, recovering more days of general conditions and interest than it cost.

Q. Under the building code, who engages the special inspector for deep foundations?

A. The owner, so the inspector is independent of the contractor.

Q. What is legally required standby power?

A. Standby power that a code or authority requires for certain loads, such as some ventilation or communication systems, held to requirements between emergency and optional standby systems. Verify against the adopted electrical code.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a formwork question arises on pour day, everyone looks for the person responsible. If the contract, the specification and the safety plan do not agree on who that is, nobody is, and the decision goes to whoever is in a hurry. Today you learn where each rule lives so you can check, before the frame starts, that every question has an owner.

OSHA: the safety floor

In plain English: federal workplace safety law requires that formwork and shoring be designed, built and inspected so they do not collapse on workers, and that they stay in place until the concrete can carry itself.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration's construction standards are in Part 1926 of Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Subpart Q covers concrete and masonry construction. It addresses formwork design so that it supports all vertical and lateral loads expected during placement, drawings or plans for formwork and shoring to be available on site, inspection of shoring before and during placement, and a requirement that forms and shores not be removed until the employer determines the concrete has gained enough strength to support its own weight and any superimposed loads, by tests or by plans and specifications [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify the current text, and any state plan that adopts or exceeds it, before relying on any provision.

OSHA's duties fall on employers, mainly the contractors whose workers are exposed. The multi-employer doctrine, which Duke taught in Week 53, can extend responsibility to controlling and creating employers on a shared site. Professional sign-off required: construction safety professional and construction lawyer for how that doctrine might apply to an owner's role.

ACI and the specification: the engineering

ACI 347, the American Concrete Institute's guide to formwork for concrete, covers design loads, materials, construction and removal of formwork. ACI also publishes guidance on shoring and reshoring of concrete buildings under construction [unverified — confirm independently]. ACI 308 covers curing, and ACI 305 and ACI 306 cover hot and cold weather. These are guides; the project specification adopts them by reference or turns them into requirements.

The structural engineer of record typically specifies the strength at which forms may be stripped and the criteria for reshoring, because those depend on the permanent structure's design. The contractor typically designs the formwork, shoring and reshoring as temporary works, a means and methods responsibility, often with its own licensed engineer. The specification should say both things plainly.

Say that out loud now.

The contract: who designs and who checks

Worked example, hypothetical. A specification says: "Formwork and reshoring are the contractor's responsibility. Forms may be removed when concrete has reached sufficient strength." Two gaps. First, sufficient is undefined; the engineer has not stated a number. Second, there is no requirement for a temporary works design, drawings on site or an independent check. Rewritten: "The contractor shall engage a licensed engineer to design formwork, shoring and reshoring, and shall submit drawings showing the shoring and reshoring sequence for review by the engineer of record for its effect on the permanent structure. Slab forms may be stripped when field-cured cylinders show at least the strength the engineer of record states on the drawings. Drawings shall be posted on site." Now each question has an owner.

A second example. The engineer's review of the reshoring drawings is for effect on the permanent structure, not an approval of the temporary works design itself. Make sure the contract says so, or the engineer may refuse to review at all, and the contractor may later argue the engineer approved its design.

Two Systems

Canada, in concept: occupational health and safety on construction sites is regulated mainly by the provinces and territories, each with its own construction safety regulations covering formwork and falsework, and design of temporary works is commonly assigned to professional engineers under provincial rules. Guyana, in concept: occupational safety and health is governed by national legislation administered by the government's labour authorities, with construction practice on larger projects often drawing on international standards and contract forms. Treat both descriptions as conceptual and verify against primary source.

What the owner must keep

The rules above produce documents, and some of them you should hold, Mr Shabazz. The temporary works design and its drawings, with the designer's stamp. The engineer of record's review letter, stating its scope. The shoring inspection records, made before and during each placement. The field-cured cylinder results for each floor, and the stripping log showing which level was stripped, when, and on which result. The reshoring drawings as revised during the job. If an incident occurs, or a slab deflects years later and someone asks how it was built, this file answers the question. Without it, the answer is a matter of recollection, which is the weakest kind of evidence there is.

Where owners go wrong

Owners sometimes try to stay out of formwork entirely, on the theory that touching it creates responsibility. Staying out of the design is right; that is the contractor's means and methods. Staying out of the evidence is not. Requiring in your contract that strength-based stripping, engineered drawings and inspection records exist, and checking that they do, is how an owner makes sure the system is running without directing how the contractor builds. Ask your lawyer to draft that boundary carefully. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.

Finally, align the documents before the frame starts. Read the safety plan, the specification section on formwork and the structural drawings side by side, and check that they name the same stripping strength, the same reshoring requirement and the same responsible parties. Where they disagree, fix it by addendum before the first slab, not by argument on the first stripping day. That review takes an afternoon and closes the gaps where accidents happen.

Keep the marked-up copies of all three documents with the review notes. If the gaps you closed are ever questioned, the marked-up set shows that the owner found them, assigned them and had them fixed before work began, which is exactly the diligence a regulator, an insurer or a court will look for after an incident.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a specification that uses words like sufficient strength and leaves temporary works design unassigned. The control is a specification that names the stripping strength, requires an engineered and drawn shoring and reshoring sequence, and states who reviews what.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the structural engineer of record designs the shores. Usually the engineer sets the criteria and the contractor's engineer designs the temporary works.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX and Marco taught order of precedence and conditions precedent in contract forms. Formwork responsibility is a precedence question in miniature: the specification, the drawings and the safety plan must agree, or the contract's precedence clause will decide in a dispute what nobody decided on site.

Recap

OSHA Subpart Q sets the safety floor for formwork and stripping, verified against current text. ACI guides and the specification set the engineering and the stripping strength. The contract assigns temporary works design to the contractor's engineer and review to the engineer of record.

Next: Duke, on The Numbers: reshoring loads and evaluating a low break with cores.
checklist: I know which OSHA standards and any state plan apply to my site.
The specification states a numeric stripping strength, not sufficient strength.
The contractor engages a licensed engineer for formwork, shoring and reshoring.
Shoring and reshoring drawings are submitted and posted on site.
The engineer of record reviews the sequence for its effect on the permanent structure.
The contract states that review is not approval of temporary works design.
The safety plan, specification and drawings agree on responsibility.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, temporary works engineer and construction safety professional.
head: Field checklist
speak: Formwork sits where three sets of rules meet. OSHA, in Subpart Q of Part 1926, sets the safety floor: formwork designed for expected loads, plans on site, shoring inspected, and forms not removed until concrete can carry its load, which I verify against current text. ACI guidance on formwork, shoring and curing, adopted through the specification, sets the engineering. The contract assigns who designs and who checks: usually the engineer of record states the stripping strength and reviews the sequence for its effect on the permanent structure, while the contractor's licensed engineer designs the temporary works. In a hypothetical specification, the phrase sufficient strength left both the number and the designer undefined. Rewritten, it named a field-cured cylinder strength, required engineered drawings posted on site and stated that review is not approval.
terms: Temporary works — structures built to support construction and later removed, such as formwork, shoring and reshoring.
Means and methods — the contractor's choice of how to carry out the work, normally its own responsibility under the contract.
Subpart Q — the part of OSHA's construction standards covering concrete and masonry construction, including formwork and shoring.

hostile.q: I'm the structural engineer of record. You want me to review the reshoring drawings. I won't take responsibility for the contractor's temporary works.
hostile.a: You will not have to, and the contract says so. Your review is limited to the effect of the shoring and reshoring sequence on the permanent structure, such as the loads on young slabs below, and it is stated not to be an approval of the temporary works design, which remains the contractor's engineer's responsibility. I need your stripping strength on the drawings and your check that the sequence does not overload the structure. That is the part only you can do.

title: Reshoring Loads and a Low Break, Step by Step
summary: Two worked calculations in hypothetical round numbers: how the load of a new slab is shared through reshored floors below, and how a low cylinder result is evaluated with cores. Both show why decisions on pour day must rest on arithmetic and evidence, not habit.
body:
The load of every new floor has to go somewhere, and the arithmetic of where it goes, through how many young slabs, is the reason reshoring rules exist and the reason a low break must be answered with evidence rather than opinion.

Recall

Q. Who typically designs formwork, shoring and reshoring?

A. The contractor, as temporary works, usually through its own licensed engineer, while the engineer of record sets the stripping strength and reviews the sequence for its effect on the permanent structure.

Q. How do you count piles under a column?

A. Total load divided by usable capacity per pile after downdrag, rounded up.

Q. In plumbing design, why does a tall building need booster pumps?

A. Because street water pressure cannot lift water to the upper floors at usable pressure, so pumps raise it, often in pressure zones.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will not design reshoring or evaluate cores, but you will be asked to approve schedule changes and decide what happens after a low break. Both calculations below are simplified so you can follow the logic. Real ones are done by the engineers and must account for the actual sequence, deflection, strength at each age and the stiffness of each floor. All numbers are hypothetical round figures in American units: psf means pounds per square foot, psi pounds per square inch.

Example one, step 1: the loads

A typical slab is 8 inches thick. Normal-weight reinforced concrete weighs about 150 pounds per cubic foot, so an 8-inch slab weighs 150 times 8 divided by 12, which is 100 psf. Formwork weighs about 10 psf. Construction live load, meaning workers, equipment and the placing process, is taken as 50 psf for this example. When the new slab is poured, the load to be carried is 100 plus 10 plus 50, which is 160 psf.

Step 2: the capacity of the floors below

Each completed slab below was designed for its own weight plus service loads, say 100 psf self-weight, 20 psf of partitions and finishes and 40 psf of live load, so 160 psf in service. But those finishes and partitions are not on yet, and the young slabs are not at full strength. For this simplified check, assume each young slab below can safely carry its own 100 psf plus an additional 60 psf of construction load at its current age, as the engineer would confirm from its strength.

Step 3: share the new load

Assume, as a simplification, that the shores and reshores share the 160 psf of new load equally among the supporting slabs below. If only 2 floors are reshored, each carries 160 divided by 2, which is 80 psf of added load: more than the 60 psf available. If 3 floors are reshored, each carries 160 divided by 3, about 53 psf: within the 60 psf limit. The engineered answer is therefore 3 levels of reshores at this stage of the cycle. Strip one level too many to free reshores for the floor above, and two slabs carry 80 psf each beyond what they can safely take.

In reality, loads do not share equally; stiffer, older slabs take more, and the engineer models that. The point of the simple version is the shape: each level of reshores you remove concentrates the load on fewer, younger slabs.

Say that out loud now.

Example two, step 1: the low break

Specified strength for a column pour is 5,000 psi. The 28-day strength test from one truck reads 4,200 psi, and the running average including it falls below specified. Under acceptance criteria that allow an individual test to fall no more than 500 psi below specified strength [unverified — confirm independently], 4,200 is 800 below, so the test fails the individual criterion. An investigation begins.

Step 2: check the testing first

The laboratory reports that this sample's cylinders sat on site for two days in hot sun before pickup. Poor initial curing lowers cylinder strength without saying anything about the column. That is a reason for doubt, not a resolution. The structural engineer checks whether 4,200 psi would satisfy the column's design. Suppose it would not, with comfortable margin, so in-place testing follows.

Step 3: cores

Three cores are drilled from the column, avoiding reinforcing steel, and tested under the governing standard. Results: 4,400, 4,100 and 4,500 psi. Average: 13,000 divided by 3, about 4,333 psi.

A common acceptance approach for cores treats the concrete as structurally adequate when the average of three cores is at least 85 percent of specified strength and no single core is below 75 percent [unverified — confirm independently]. Eighty-five percent of 5,000 is 4,250; the average of 4,333 passes. Seventy-five percent of 5,000 is 3,750; the lowest core, 4,100, passes. On that approach the column would be considered adequate, and the engineer documents the conclusion. Verify the criteria in the adopted edition of ACI 318. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.

Step 4: the cost of the answer

Cores, testing and engineering, hypothetically 8,000 dollars, and a patch of the core holes. If the cores had failed, the options would be load testing, strengthening or removal, each far more expensive. Even when the answer is good news, record who paid for the investigation; many specifications put that cost on the contractor when the concrete is found deficient and on the owner when it is found adequate.

What the arithmetic tells the owner

Two practical conclusions, Mr Shabazz. First, reshoring levels are a resource as real as forms: if the cycle is short, more levels of young concrete need support at once, and the contractor must own enough reshores to keep them all. When a schedule tightens, ask whether the reshore inventory has grown with it. A crew short of reshores is a crew tempted to pull them early.

Second, every low-break investigation should end with a written conclusion and a cost decision, filed with the pour records. If the structure is adequate, say so in a letter from the engineer, so that a future buyer's engineer reading the low cylinder result also reads why it was accepted. If it is not, the letter defines the remedy. An investigation that ends in a phone call leaves the low break on the record with no answer beside it, and the question will be asked again at sale, when the engineer who knew the answer may no longer be available.

A last check on any arithmetic you are shown: ask what was assumed. Reshoring calculations depend on the construction live load, the strength of each young slab at its age and how load actually shares. Core evaluations depend on the criteria in the adopted code edition and on cores taken and tested correctly. When an engineer gives you a conclusion, ask for those assumptions in one paragraph. It is not distrust; it is the record that lets the conclusion be checked later.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is removing reshores to speed the next floor without checking the loads they were carrying. The control is a reshoring sequence drawing, with the number of levels at each stage, posted on site and followed.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a passing core result as proof the original cylinders were wrong. Cores answer whether the structure is adequate; they do not settle why the cylinder was low.

Callback

In Week 111, Greta taught downdrag: a load nobody designed for, arriving from a layer people forgot. Reshoring loads are the same idea in the air: a construction load the permanent design never sees, carried by young slabs that must be checked for it.

Recap

A new 8-inch slab with forms and construction load is about 160 psf. Sharing it over 3 reshored floors keeps each young slab within its limit; over 2, it does not. A low break is checked through testing, design margin and cores, with core criteria verified in the adopted code.

Next: Duke, on The Room: the 5 a.m. pour-day go or no-go.
checklist: I can estimate a slab's self-weight from its thickness.
I know the construction loads assumed in the reshoring design.
The reshoring drawing shows the number of levels at each stage of the cycle.
No reshore level is removed outside that sequence.
A low break starts with a check of the testing, then the design margin.
Cores are evaluated against criteria verified in the adopted code.
The engineer documents the conclusion of every low-break investigation.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and temporary works engineer.
head: Field checklist
speak: First, reshoring. An 8-inch slab weighs about 100 psf; with 10 of formwork and 50 of construction load, a new pour puts 160 psf onto the floors below. If each young slab can safely take 60 psf extra at its age, sharing over 2 reshored floors gives 80 each, too much; over 3 floors, about 53 each, within the limit. So the sequence needs 3 levels, and removing one early overloads the others. Second, a low break. Against 5,000 psi, a test of 4,200 fails the individual check. First I check the testing: those cylinders sat in the sun. Then the design margin. Then cores: 4,400, 4,100 and 4,500 average 4,333, above 85 percent of specified, and none below 75 percent, so on that approach the column is adequate. The engineer documents it.
terms: Construction live load — the temporary load from workers, equipment and placing activity assumed during construction.
Core — a cylinder of hardened concrete drilled from the structure and tested to measure in-place strength.
Load sharing — the distribution of a construction load through shores and reshores to several slabs below.

hostile.q: I'm the formwork foreman. We need those bottom reshores for the next floor up. Why can't we pull them today?
hostile.a: Because the drawing says three levels stay under the slab we pour tomorrow, and the arithmetic is why. Spread over three floors, each young slab takes about 53 pounds per square foot extra, inside its limit. Spread over two, it is about 80, past it. If you need more reshores to keep the cycle, I will fund additional reshores this week. Pull a level outside the sequence and I stop the pour.

title: The 5 a.m. Pour-Day Go or No-Go
summary: It is 5 a.m. on a slab pour day. The forecast says extreme heat by noon, one embed is missing a signature on the pour card, the pump is late and the trucks are booked. In the room are the superintendent, the placing foreman, the inspector, the supplier's dispatcher and the MEP foreman. The lesson is how to make a clean go or no-go decision quickly and calmly.
body:
A pour-day decision is binary and the clock is loud, so the owner's job is to apply criteria agreed in advance, quickly, and to make the no-go option feel as normal as the go, because a crew that thinks stopping is failure will pour into a problem.

Recall

Q. In the reshoring example, why did 3 levels work when 2 did not?

A. Because sharing 160 psf over 3 young slabs put about 53 psf extra on each, within the 60 psf limit, while 2 levels put 80 psf on each, past it.

Q. What should you open with in a meeting after a low pile load test?

A. The one decision required: the design production piles will follow and the evidence that will confirm it.

Q. In MEP design, why does humidity control matter separately from temperature in a hot-humid climate?

A. Because a system can cool air without removing enough moisture, leaving rooms cold and clammy, with condensation and mould risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most pour problems are not engineering puzzles. They are early-morning decisions made by tired people with trucks on the road. The best defence is a short list of go or no-go criteria written before the day and agreed by everyone, so that the decision at 5 a.m. is an application of rules, not a debate. Your role as owner is rarely to make the call yourself. It is to make sure the call is made by the right person against the right criteria, and to back a no-go when it comes.

The scene

Hypothetical. A 300 cubic yard slab pour is booked for 6 a.m. The forecast shows temperatures rising fast, with a hot wind by late morning. The specification limits concrete temperature at placement and calls for evaporation control and immediate curing. The pour card is signed except for one line: the electrical foreman has not signed for a set of embedded conduits near a column, because two runs were changed last night. The pump has broken down on the highway and its replacement will arrive at 7:30. The supplier's dispatcher has trucks batching at 5:45.

The question behind the question

The superintendent asks, "Can we start with the bucket and crane until the pump arrives?" The question behind it is: can we keep the day? The dispatcher asks, "Do I keep batching?" The question behind it is: who pays for loads that get turned away? The electrical foreman says little; the question behind his silence is: will I be blamed if I hold the pour?

The lines to say

Start with the criteria, not opinions. "Three items on our go list today: the pour card fully signed, a placing method that keeps the planned rate, and a heat plan that keeps us inside the temperature and curing limits. Let's go through them."

To the dispatcher, first, because his trucks are the clock: "Hold batching for thirty minutes. We will call you by 5:45 with a go, a delayed start or a cancel." Holding is cheaper than turning trucks away.

To the electrical foreman: "What do you need to sign, and how long will it take?" If the answer is fifteen minutes to check the two changed runs, give him fifteen minutes. If it is unknown, the item is open.

To the superintendent: "Can a crane and bucket keep the planned placing rate so we don't get a cold joint, a seam where fresh concrete meets concrete that has already begun to set? If not, we wait for the pump."

Say that out loud now.

A worked decision

Run the numbers. With the pump at 7:30 and a placing rate of 60 cubic yards an hour, 300 cubic yards take 5 hours, finishing around 12:30, in the hottest part of the day, under a hot wind. Concrete temperature limits and evaporation will be hard to hold in the last two hours. The plant can supply chilled water and a retarder, and the crew has evaporation retarder and curing materials on site. Option one: start at 7:30 with heat measures, accept the late finish. Option two: split the pour at a construction joint the engineer has already approved, placing half today and half tomorrow at 5 a.m. Option three: cancel and pour the whole slab tomorrow at 5 a.m.

The criteria decide. If the conduit check is complete and a pre-approved joint exists, option two keeps most of the day and avoids the worst heat. If the conduit check is not complete, nothing pours over that column today; option two can still work if the joint lies short of it, otherwise option three. Write the decision and the reason on the pour card. Tell the dispatcher by 5:45.

The lines never to say

"Just sign it, we'll fix it later." Nothing embedded can be fixed later without cutting structure.

"We've poured in worse heat." Experience is not a temperature limit.

"Whose fault is the pump?" Not now. Fault is for the afternoon.

When to stay silent

After asking the electrical foreman what he needs, wait. He is the person most likely to be pressured into signing early, and your silence tells the room his answer matters. Stay silent again after the superintendent proposes the crane. Let him run the placing-rate arithmetic himself; he will often reach the right answer faster than you could push him to it.

Holding your state

Five in the morning, Mr Shabazz, is a familiar hour from shift work, and you know what it does to judgment: the body is near its low point and urgency feels larger than it is. Eat something before you arrive. Keep the go list on paper in your pocket. Speak slowly, and if the room speeds up, slow your own voice further. Any breathing reset happens parked in your vehicle before you walk onto the deck, never while driving. A calm no-go at 5:40 is a better morning than a rushed go at 5:30.

After the decision

Once the call is made, the morning still needs managing. Tell the whole crew, not only the foremen, what was decided and why, in two sentences, so nobody spends the morning speculating. If the pour is split, confirm the joint location on the deck with the superintendent and the inspector, and photograph it. Record the start time, the placing rate, the concrete temperatures and when curing began. Thank the electrical foreman publicly for holding his signature until he had checked the runs. That last act costs nothing, and it tells every trade on the job that an honest hold is welcome, which is the behaviour that keeps embedded defects out of your building.

Later that day, write a short note for the file: what went wrong, what the criteria said, what was decided, and one change for next time, perhaps a backup pump arrangement on large pours or an earlier cut-off for design changes to embeds.

Over a career of pours, that small note becomes a library of what went wrong on mornings like this, and it is the best training material your future site teams will ever have.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a go decision driven by trucks already on the road. The control is a go list agreed before pour day, a dispatcher hold rule, and a pre-approved construction joint that makes a partial pour a normal option.

The beginner's mistake

Making the call yourself because you are the owner. The superintendent makes the call; you make sure it is made against the criteria and you back a no-go.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught OODA: observe, orient, decide, act. A pour morning is OODA under a clock. The go list is your orientation, prepared in advance, so the decision can be fast without being careless.

Recap

Apply agreed criteria: full pour card, a placing method that holds the rate, a heat plan inside the limits. Hold batching before turning trucks away. Use a pre-approved joint to split a pour. Never sign over an open embed. Back the no-go.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: Week 113 review, concrete in the field.
checklist: A written go or no-go list is agreed before pour day.
The supplier's dispatcher has a hold rule and a call deadline.
No pour proceeds over an unsigned line on the pour card.
I check that the placing method keeps the rate and avoids cold joints.
A heat or cold plan keeps concrete within its temperature and curing limits.
A pre-approved construction joint makes a partial pour a normal option.
The decision and its reason are written on the pour card.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record for any construction joint location.
head: Field checklist
speak: On pour day the clock is loud, so I apply criteria agreed in advance. Three items: the pour card fully signed, a placing method that keeps the rate and avoids cold joints, and a heat plan that keeps the concrete inside its temperature and curing limits. First I tell the dispatcher to hold batching for thirty minutes, because holding is cheaper than turning trucks away. I ask the electrical foreman what he needs to sign and give him the time. In a hypothetical case, a late pump means 300 yards at 60 an hour finishing in the worst heat, so the better option is to pour half today to an engineer-approved joint and half tomorrow at dawn. Nothing pours over an unsigned embed. The superintendent makes the call; I make sure it follows the criteria, and I back a no-go.
terms: Cold joint — a weak seam formed when fresh concrete is placed against concrete that has already begun to set.
Construction joint — a planned stopping point in a pour, located and detailed by the engineer, where the next pour can bond properly.
Evaporation retarder — a liquid sprayed on fresh concrete to slow water loss from the surface before final finishing and curing.

hostile.q: I'm the ready-mix dispatcher. Your crew held my trucks for thirty minutes and then split the pour. Who pays for the batched loads I couldn't deliver?
hostile.a: The hold was called before batching, at 5:15, under the dispatch terms we agreed at the pre-construction meeting, so nothing should have been batched for those slots. Any load batched after the hold call is a matter for your dispatch log. For the loads delivered today the pour went ahead, and tomorrow's half is ordered now. If you have a load that was batched before our call, send me the ticket with the time stamp and we will settle it under the contract.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 113 Review: From the Chute to the Structure
summary: Six questions on concrete in the field, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical pour card and stripping note with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a good mix becomes good structure only through a verified pre-pour inspection, careful placing and curing, and stripping and reshoring that follow measured strength, never the calendar.

Recall

Q. On pour day, what are the three go criteria?

A. A fully signed pour card, a placing method that keeps the planned rate, and a heat or cold plan that keeps the concrete within its temperature and curing limits.

Q. What does Rule 111 require?

A. When a foundation depends on predicted long-term settlement, an independent review of the full range, monitoring against written triggers, and action on the first evidence before occupancy and sale.

Q. What is integrated systems testing in commissioning?

A. Testing how building systems work together, such as fire alarm, smoke control, elevators and power, under real scenarios, rather than each system alone.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six without notes, you can stand on a deck on pour morning and follow every decision. Answer each aloud first.

The six questions

Question 1. What does a pre-pour inspection check, and why is it the owner's best leverage?

Answer: Forms, reinforcing, cover, embeds, sleeves and cleanliness, signed by each responsible party. It is the last moment anything buried can be fixed cheaply.

Question 2. What is curing, and what happens without it?

Answer: Keeping concrete moist and at a suitable temperature so the cement keeps reacting. Without it the surface loses strength, shrinks, cracks and becomes more permeable.

Question 3. What was the root cause of the Skyline Towers collapse in 1973?

Answer: Removing support from a young floor on time rather than on verified strength, without in-place evidence or an enforced reshoring plan, in cold weather that slowed strength gain.

Question 4. What does a day on the floor cycle cost, and what is often a better trade than stripping early?

Answer: General conditions plus interest on the drawn loan. A second form set or weather measures usually recover more time than they cost.

Question 5. Who typically designs shoring and reshoring, and what does the engineer of record do?

Answer: The contractor's licensed engineer designs the temporary works. The engineer of record states the stripping strength and reviews the sequence for its effect on the permanent structure.

Question 6. A new pour puts 160 psf on the floors below, and each young slab can take 60 psf extra. How many reshored levels are needed if load shares equally?

Answer: Two levels give 80 psf each, too much; three give about 53 psf each. Three levels.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Duke framed the pour as decided before the first truck. Ford took Skyline Towers through seven steps, giving Rule 113. Roman priced the floor cycle against a tear-out. REGA set out OSHA, ACI and contract responsibility for temporary works. Duke ran the reshoring and core arithmetic. Duke ran the 5 a.m. go or no-go.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical pour card and stripping note. Find the defects before reading on.

Pour card, Level 6 slab. Formwork: OK. Reinforcing: OK, inspected by rebar foreman. Cover: as per drawings. Embeds: electrical, to be confirmed after pour. Plumbing sleeves: signed. Special inspector: signature pending, pour may proceed. Weather: hot, curing compound to be applied next morning. Stripping note: Level 5 forms to be stripped Thursday, day 4, per schedule. Reshores: remove Level 3 reshores Thursday to reuse on Level 7.

The defects. First, reinforcing inspected by the rebar foreman, not the special inspector, whose signature is pending, yet the card says the pour may proceed. Second, cover recorded as per drawings rather than measured. Third, electrical embeds to be confirmed after the pour, which is impossible without cutting structure. Fourth, curing deferred to the next morning on a hot day, inviting plastic shrinkage cracks and a weak surface. Fifth, stripping set by schedule, day 4, with no reference to field-cured cylinder strength, the exact mechanism of Skyline Towers. Sixth, reshores removed from Level 3 to reuse above, with no reference to the reshoring drawing, which may require that level to remain. Seventh, no signature line for the person who decided any of it.

The corrected version: every line signed by its responsible party, including the special inspector; cover measured and recorded; embeds confirmed before the pour; curing started immediately after finishing; stripping only on field-cured results against the engineer's strength; reshores removed only per the posted sequence.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why does the concrete frame cost what it costs, and where can it go wrong?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "A concrete frame is one floor built many times, so its cost and schedule hang on the floor cycle. Each pour starts with a pre-pour inspection, because everything inside the slab is buried for good. During the pour the crew places and vibrates the concrete properly and starts curing at once, which protects strength and durability. After the pour, the young slab is held up by shores and reshores, and forms come off only when field-cured cylinders show the strength the engineer requires, never on a fixed number of days, because cold weather slows strength gain and stripping early is how frames have collapsed. When weather slows us, we buy time safely with extra form sets or weather measures, which cost far less than a tear-out. And a low break is answered with evidence: check the testing, check the design, take cores if needed."

Score your answer: bottom line first, pre-pour and curing named, strength-based stripping explained, a safe way to recover time, inside two minutes. If not, record it again tomorrow.

Self-test before you move on

Kema's check, Mr Shabazz. On a card, without looking back, write the life of a pour in order: pre-pour inspection and signatures, go or no-go criteria, placing and consolidation, finishing, curing, field-cured cylinders, stripping at the engineer's strength, reshoring per the posted sequence, and the records each step leaves behind. Then write Rule 113 in your own words. If both take under two minutes, the week has landed.

Then link the last three weeks into one chain, because they are one subject. Week 111 put the building on piles proven by tests and records. Week 112 made the concrete with an approved recipe and proved its strength and durability. Week 113 turned that concrete into structure through inspection, curing and strength-based support. In all three, the material disappears from view and the evidence is the only inspection left. Carry that sentence into Bram's week on steel, where the same idea applies to bolts and welds.

One habit for your next site visit: ask for the stripping log and the reshoring drawing, and walk the floor below the newest slab to see that the reshores match the drawing. It takes ten minutes, it needs no engineering knowledge, and it is the single check that most directly tests whether Rule 113 is being followed on your job.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is schedule pressure overriding evidence on the deck. The control is a written go list, a strength-based stripping rule and a posted reshoring sequence.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the pour card as paperwork. It is the last inspection of everything inside the structure.

Callback

In Week 112, Ingrid taught that cylinders prove the delivered mix, not the placed concrete. This week showed the rest of that sentence: placement, curing and support decide whether the delivered mix becomes the structure the engineer designed.

Recap

Pre-pour inspection, proper placing and immediate curing make the structure. Stripping and reshoring follow verified strength and an engineered sequence. Weather measures and form sets buy time safely. Low breaks are answered with evidence. Rule 113 keeps the calendar out of stripping.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, concrete in the field. Every pour starts with a pre-pour inspection signed by each party, because forms, steel, cover and embeds are buried for good. The crew places and vibrates concrete without separation and starts curing at once, especially in heat. Young slabs are carried by shores and reshores, and forms come off only when field-cured cylinders show the engineer's stripping strength. Skyline Towers in 1973 showed what happens otherwise, and gave Rule 113: never strip on the calendar. A day on the floor cycle costs general conditions plus interest, so I buy time safely with form sets and weather measures, which cost far less than a tear-out. A low break gets evidence: testing, design margin, then cores. On pour day, agreed go criteria decide, and I back a no-go.
terms: Pour card — a pre-pour checklist signed by each responsible party confirming the work to be buried is ready for concrete.
Plastic shrinkage cracking — surface cracks that form within hours when fresh concrete loses water faster than it rises to the surface.
Honeycombing — voids in hardened concrete where paste failed to fill around the stone, usually from poor consolidation.

hostile.q: I'm the lender's monitor. Your Level 6 pour card shows the special inspector's signature as pending. Why should I certify that slab?
hostile.a: You should not until the gap is closed, and I have already stopped the next pour on that basis. The special inspector has been asked for the reinforcing report for Level 6, including the cover measurements. If it shows the steel and cover were right, it closes the card. If not, the structural engineer evaluates the slab, with cover-meter readings and cores if needed, and I report the outcome and any remedy in the next package. From today, no truck is called until every signature is on the card.
